sceneHappening: Lazarus dies in Bethany, and Jesus calls him out of the tomb
summary: A man named Lazarus is sick, from Bethany, the village of Mary and her sister Martha. The sisters send to Jesus, "Lord, behold, he for whom you have great affection is sick." Jesus says, "This sickness is not to death, but for the glory of God, that God's Son may be glorified by it." John says Jesus loved Martha, her sister, and Lazarus, but when he hears Lazarus is sick, he stays two days in the place where he is. Then he says to the disciples, "Let's go into Judea again." They say, "Rabbi, the Jews were just trying to stone you; are you going there again?" He says, "Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I am going so that I may awake him out of sleep." They think he means natural sleep, so he tells them plainly, "Lazarus is dead. I am glad for your sakes that I was not there, to the intent that you may believe." Thomas, who is called Didymus, says to his fellow disciples, "Let's also go, that we may die with him." Jesus comes to find that Lazarus has been in the tomb four days already. Bethany is near Jerusalem, about two miles away, and many of the Jews have come to Martha and Mary to console them. When Martha hears that Jesus is coming, she goes and meets him: "Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn't have died. Even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you." "Your brother will rise again." "I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day." Jesus says, "I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me, though he dies, yet will he live. Whoever lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?" She says, "Yes, Lord. I have come to believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, he who comes into the world." She calls her sister Mary secretly, saying, "The Teacher is here and is calling you." Mary gets up quickly and goes to him, and the Jews who were with her in the house, following her, think she is going to the tomb to weep there. Mary falls at his feet: "Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn't have died." When Jesus sees her weeping, and the Jews weeping who came with her, "he groaned in the spirit, and was troubled," and asks, "Where have you laid him?" "Lord, come and see." "Jesus wept." The Jews say, "See how much affection he had for him!" and some, "Couldn't this man, who opened the eyes of him who was blind, have also kept this man from dying?" Jesus, again groaning in himself, comes to the tomb, a cave with a stone laid against it. "Take away the stone." Martha says, "Lord, by this time there is a stench, for he has been dead four days." "Didn't I tell you that if you believed, you would see God's glory?" They take away the stone. Jesus lifts up his eyes and says, "Father, I thank you that you listened to me. I know that you always listen to me, but because of the multitude standing around I said this, that they may believe that you sent me." He cries with a loud voice, "Lazarus, come out!" The one who was dead comes out, his hands and feet bound with graveclothes, and his face wrapped in a cloth. Jesus says, "Free him, and let him go." Many of the Jews who came to Mary and saw what he did believe in him, but some go to the Pharisees and tell them. The chief priests and the Pharisees gather the council: "What are we doing? For this man does many signs. If we leave him alone like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation." One of them, Caiaphas, being high priest that year, says, "You know nothing at all, nor do you consider that it is advantageous for you that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation not perish." John comments that he said this not of himself but, as high priest, prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but that he might gather together into one the children of God who are scattered abroad. From that day they plan to put him to death. Jesus therefore walks no more openly among the Jews, but goes to a country near the wilderness, to a city called Ephraim, and stays there with his disciples. The Passover is near, and many go up to Jerusalem to purify themselves, and they seek Jesus, asking, "What do you think? Won't he come to the feast at all?"
whySettingMatters: Bethany lay on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives about two miles from Jerusalem, so the sisters' village was close enough for many Jerusalem mourners to come, and close enough that the miracle was seen. Lazarus' four days in the tomb matter: later Jewish tradition held that the soul stayed near the body for three days, so four days meant there was no hope; John makes sure it is clear that Lazarus was truly dead. "Jesus wept" (11:35) is the shortest verse in many English Bibles and uses a word for quiet weeping. His "groaning" is a word that can mean anger or deep disturbance, and why he is moved is debated; it could be grief, anger at death, or at the unbelief around him. Martha's confession (11:27) is the counterpart to Peter's in the other Gospels. Graveclothes bound each limb and the face was wrapped in a cloth. Caiaphas was high priest from about AD 18 to 36, and it was his job to keep order with Rome; his words, "one man should die for the people," are meant politically, and John reads them as an unwitting prophecy. The Sanhedrin's fear of the Romans is realistic. Ephraim was a village north of Jerusalem on the edge of the wilderness. Thomas' courage in 11:16 is often overlooked next to his doubt in chapter 20.

questions: Jesus waits two days after hearing Lazarus is sick. What do you make of the delay?
Martha says she knows her brother will rise "at the last day," and Jesus says, "I am the resurrection." What changes between those two?
"Jesus wept." Why does he weep when he is about to raise Lazarus?
Caiaphas says one man should die for the people. What does John see in that statement?
